chapter: Race, unions and the color line
title: Wingy Manone, Tweedy and Bobby Hackett
summary: Short exchanges on a one-armed trumpeter Wingy Manone, Tweedy, and a visit by Bobby Hackett to the Famous Door.

story.theme_name: Remembering the early trumpeters and their styles
story.community_name: Trumpeters I admired: rating the horn players

blocks.x: And I knew Brian Gilbert for a long time. I didn't really know him. He was a young man. What about the one-armed trumpet player?
What was his name? Tweedy? Tweedy, yeah.
Oh, Tweedy. Did you know Tweedy, John? Tweedy was a young fella. I know, Wiggy Malone.
No, he's young. He was young, but young.
Wiggy was a young guy. Yeah, Wiggy was young at that time. There was a place called Plug 51 in Wiggy, by 1940.
That was way back there. You only hear Wiggy recently, Johnny. Yeah, to the record. Better than that one.
I read him down here when he was down here about three years ago. He was on Bourbon Street, somewhere down Bourbon. I don't know.

He used to sit down at the famous door a few times. I heard him down there. But he never done nothing I thought was great. I don't know. But then he was probably loaded every time I heard him. I don't know, man. Did he hear Hackett, too, when he was down there? Pardon? Bobby Hackett. No, I didn't hear him. As a matter of fact, I'm Mr. Abe Lincoln. My idol with the trombone. He comes down for one night, sits in at the famous door, and I ain't there that day.
Well, I could play pretty. But he's a fast man. I'm a good girl.
